spark.title: Latency vs. Throughput
spark.summary: Understand how per-request latency (p50/p95/p99) and system-wide throughput (RPS/QPS) interact via Little's Law, and why pushing utilization past the knee destroys tail latency.
spark.keyTakeaway: Aim for maximal throughput while keeping tail latency (p99) within your SLO budget; batching boosts throughput at the cost of per-item latency.
spark.byteSummary:
Understand how per-request latency (p50/p95/p99) and system-wide throughput (RPS/QPS) interact via Little's Law, and why pushing utilization past the knee destroys tail latency.

A system can average 5ms latency at 100 RPS yet collapse to 2,000ms p99 latency at 850 RPS because queueing delay grows non-linearly near saturation.

Aim for maximal throughput while keeping tail latency (p99) within your SLO budget; batching boosts throughput at the cost of per-item latency.

concept.whyItMatters: A system can average 5ms latency at 100 RPS yet collapse to 2,000ms p99 latency at 850 RPS because queueing delay grows non-linearly near saturation. Knowing [Little's Law](/concept/capacity-planning-forecasting) ($L = \lambda W$) and tail-latency amplification lets you size worker pools, tune batch sizes, and enforce [backpressure](/concept/backpressure-flow-control) before queues explode.
whenToUse: Optimizing interactive APIs where p99 user-facing latency matters most (parallel fan-out, hedged requests, smaller payloads).
Optimizing offline/streaming pipelines where throughput matters most (micro-batching, compression, async group commit).
whenNotToUse: Using arithmetic mean (average) latency instead of p95/p99 percentiles—averages hide severe tail stalls affecting your busiest users.
keyPoints: Latency is the duration to complete a single operation (ms); throughput is the rate of completed operations per unit time (RPS, MB/s).
Little's Law relates concurrency $L$, arrival rate $\lambda$, and average latency $W$: $L = \lambda \times W$.
As server utilization $\rho$ approaches 100%, M/M/1 queueing wait time scales as $\frac{\rho}{1 - \rho}$, causing exponential p99 spikes.
Tail-at-scale effect: if a request fans out to $N=20$ microservices each with 1% slow responses, the chance of at least one slow sub-call is $1 - 0.99^{20} \approx 18.2\%$.

sections.content:
## Architecture & Trade-Off Matrix

| Metric / Lever | Effect on Latency | Effect on Throughput | Production Trade-Off |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Micro-batching** | Increases (waits to fill batch) | Increases sharply (amortizes syscalls) | Great for Kafka/logs; bad for interactive RPC |
| **Parallel Fan-Out** | Decreases (concurrent sub-calls) | Increases thread/socket load | Vulnerable to tail-latency amplification |
| **Connection Pooling** | Decreases (skips TCP/TLS handshake) | Increases | Must bound pool size to avoid DB saturation |
| **Load Shedding (429)** | Protects p99 for admitted traffic | Caps accepted RPS safely | Prevents cascading queue collapse |

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
